data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The nocturnal UHI is fundamentally an inversion-geometry effect: dense city streets act as topographic basins that pool cold air, but deep street canyons slow the vertical sensible heat exchange, trapping daytime heat near the surface; the cross-city variance depends strictly on the threshold where canyon trapping exceeds cold-air pooling.","counterconditions":[{"case":"Lidar and drone measurements show no persistent cold-air pooling in urban street canyons, and vertical temperature profiles show continuous lapse rates rather than trapped inversions.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The nocturnal UHI gap is entirely explained by differences in ground-level soil moisture without any dependence on building height or canyon geometry.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"Removing the topographic basin effect in wind-tunnel models does not reduce the nocturnal UHI.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The UHI is consistently stronger in flat, sprawling cities than in cities situated in topographic basins.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Unlike the open countryside, which cools rapidly as cold, dense air drains away or forms a surface inversion, deep urban street canyons physically block the horizontal advection of cold air and slow vertical turbulent mixing. This traps the warmer, daytime air within the urban canopy layer. The mechanism transitions from cold-air pooling (which would make cities colder) to heat trapping (which makes them warmer) depending on the building height and street width.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
